facts.title: The Taj Changes Color
facts.description: It appears pink in the morning, bright white in the day, and golden at sunset due to sunlight reflecting on the marble.

facts.title: Almost Perfectly Symmetrical
facts.description: The entire complex is symmetrical except one detail: Shah Jahan’s tomb is slightly off-center next to Mumtaz Mahal’s.

facts.title: Optical Illusion in Calligraphy
facts.description: The Quranic calligraphy looks uniform, but the letters are bigger at the top so it appears perfectly aligned from the ground.

No touching or scratching marble surfaces

facts.title: The Only Visitor Entrance Today
facts.description: Public entry to Agra Fort is currently through Amar Singh Gate, while other parts of the fort remain restricted.

facts.title: Once Called Akbar Darwaza
facts.description: The southern gateway was historically known as Akbar Darwaza before becoming known as Amar Singh Gate.

facts.title: Built to Slow an Attacking Army
facts.description: Its angled approach, rising ramp and defensive turns made it difficult for attacking elephants or troops to charge directly into the fort.

items: This is the main public entrance to Agra Fort
Notice the curved defensive approach while walking inside
groups.title: At Amar Singh Gate

audio.title: Amar Singh Gate: Entering the Mughal Fortress

description: Amar Singh Gate is the southern gateway of Agra Fort and the entrance used by visitors today. Built during Akbar's reconstruction of the fort, its rising and turning approach reflects the defensive planning of a major Mughal fortress.

facts.title: Its Name Means Garden of Grapes
facts.description: Anguri Bagh is commonly translated as the Garden of Grapes and formed part of the private palace landscape.

facts.title: Geometry Was Part of the Beauty
facts.description: The garden is arranged as a carefully ordered Mughal garden with geometric planting beds, pathways and water features.

facts.title: Connected to Khas Mahal
facts.description: The garden lies directly beside Khas Mahal and formed an intimate landscaped courtyard for the surrounding royal apartments.

items: View the garden from the surrounding paths
Notice its geometric layout from a slightly elevated position
groups.title: At Anguri Bagh

audio.title: Anguri Bagh: The Garden of Grapes

description: Anguri Bagh is the formal garden beside Khas Mahal. Its geometric beds, pathways and water features formed a carefully ordered landscape within Shah Jahan's private palace quarters.

facts.title: Court Open to the Public
facts.description: Diwan-i-Am means Hall of Public Audience and was where the emperor received subjects and heard petitions.

facts.title: Created Early in Shah Jahan's Reign
facts.description: The hall was begun soon after Shah Jahan became emperor and belongs to the major palace works of his reign.

facts.title: A Throne Chamber Overlooked the Hall
facts.description: The emperor occupied an elevated throne area while officials and petitioners assembled in the audience hall and courtyard.

items: Stand back to understand the scale of the audience hall
Look for the emperor's elevated throne area
Do not climb onto protected architectural elements
groups.title: At Diwan-i-Am

audio.title: Diwan-i-Am: Where the Emperor Heard the People

description: Diwan-i-Am is Agra Fort's Hall of Public Audience. Built for Shah Jahan, the large columned hall provided a formal setting where the emperor appeared before the court, received petitions and conducted public affairs.

facts.title: For the Empire's Most Important Guests
facts.description: Diwan-i-Khas was the Hall of Private Audience, where the emperor received nobles, ambassadors and other important visitors.

facts.title: A Marble Hall Open on Three Sides
facts.description: The hall was designed with five arched openings supported by paired columns and was open on three sides.

facts.title: Once Richly Gilded
facts.description: Historical descriptions record a wooden ceiling decorated with gold and silver leaf, while the marble surfaces carried refined floral carving and inlay.

items: Notice the paired columns and open-sided pavilion design
Look closely at surviving floral carving and marble work
groups.title: At Diwan-i-Khas

audio.title: Diwan-i-Khas: Inside the Emperor's Private Court

description: Diwan-i-Khas is the Hall of Private Audience built for Shah Jahan. Smaller and more intimate than Diwan-i-Am, it provided an elegant setting for meetings with nobles, ambassadors and important representatives of the Mughal state.

facts.title: Built During Akbar's Reign
facts.description: Despite its name, Jahangiri Mahal belongs to the surviving palace architecture created during Emperor Akbar's reconstruction of Agra Fort.

facts.title: A Palace for the Royal Household
facts.description: The building formed part of the residential palace complex and is traditionally associated with the women of the Mughal royal household.

facts.title: The Giant Stone Basin
facts.description: A large monolithic stone basin known as Hauz-i-Jahangiri stands near the palace and bears a Persian inscription.

items: Look for the mixture of red sandstone carving and different architectural traditions
Notice the large stone Hauz-i-Jahangiri nearby
Do not touch carved heritage surfaces
groups.title: At Jahangiri Mahal

description: Jahangiri Mahal is one of the most important surviving palace buildings from Akbar's Agra Fort. Built primarily in red sandstone, it preserves the robust architectural character of Akbar's period and formed part of the imperial residential quarters.

facts.title: Shah Jahan Changed the Fort's Look
facts.description: Khas Mahal represents Shah Jahan's preference for elegant white marble, contrasting strongly with Akbar's earlier red-sandstone palaces.

facts.title: Garden on One Side, River on the Other
facts.description: The palace occupies a privileged location between Anguri Bagh and the Yamuna-facing side of Agra Fort.

facts.title: A Private Royal Retreat
facts.description: Khas Mahal functioned as part of the emperor's private residential quarters and is also known as an aramgah, or place of rest.

items: Compare its white marble with Akbar's red-sandstone buildings
Look toward Anguri Bagh from the palace side
Do not touch marble or decorative surfaces
groups.title: At Khas Mahal

audio.title: Khas Mahal: Shah Jahan's Marble Retreat

description: Khas Mahal is a refined marble palace created during Shah Jahan's transformation of Agra Fort. Positioned between the Yamuna-facing palaces and Anguri Bagh, it formed part of the emperor's private residential world.

facts.title: Its Name May Be Misleading
facts.description: Machchi Bhawan means 'Fish House' or 'Fish Square', but the Mughal chronicle Badshahnama describes rooms here as a treasury for imperial ornaments and jewels.

facts.title: Once Filled with Water Features
facts.description: The courtyard historically contained elaborate water features, including channels, fountains and tanks that have largely disappeared.

facts.title: Part of Shah Jahan's Palace World
facts.description: The large courtyard connects closely with major palace structures including Diwan-i-Khas, the royal baths and Nagina Masjid.

items: Observe the courtyard from permitted visitor levels
Imagine the former fountains, tanks and water channels
Some lower areas may not be publicly accessible
groups.title: At Machchi Bhawan

audio.title: Machchi Bhawan: Fish Square or Imperial Treasury?

description: Machchi Bhawan is a large palace courtyard within Shah Jahan's section of Agra Fort. Although its name suggests a connection with fish tanks, historical descriptions also identify its lower rooms with the storage of imperial jewels and ornaments. The courtyard once contained elaborate fountains and water channels.

facts.title: An Octagonal Marble Tower
facts.description: Musamman Burj is an octagonal tower and open pavilion built during Shah Jahan's marble transformation of Agra Fort.

facts.title: Shah Jahan's Final Years
facts.description: Tradition strongly associates the tower with Shah Jahan's confinement during his final years after Aurangzeb took power.

facts.title: A View Toward the Taj Mahal
facts.description: Its river-facing position provides one of Agra Fort's most famous views toward the Taj Mahal across the Yamuna.

items: Look east across the Yamuna for the Taj Mahal
Notice the marble jali and inlay work
Remain behind barriers near river-facing edges
groups.title: At Musamman Burj

audio.title: Musamman Burj: Shah Jahan's View of the Taj

description: Musamman Burj is an octagonal marble tower and pavilion on Agra Fort's river-facing side. Built during Shah Jahan's reign, it is traditionally remembered as the place where the deposed emperor spent his final years with a view toward the Taj Mahal.

facts.title: The Gem Mosque
facts.description: Nagina Masjid is also known as the Gem Mosque, reflecting the small building's refined white-marble appearance.

facts.title: A Private Royal Mosque
facts.description: Shah Jahan built the mosque within the private palace zone, where it was associated with worship by members of the imperial household.

facts.title: Three Marble Domes
facts.description: Its compact prayer chamber is crowned by three domes and fronted by three elegant cusped arches.

items: Respect the structure as a historic mosque
Avoid disturbing worship if taking place
groups.title: At Nagina Masjid

description: Nagina Masjid is a small white-marble mosque built during Shah Jahan's reign within Agra Fort's private palace area. Its restrained design, three-domed prayer chamber and delicate arches distinguish it from the fort's larger ceremonial buildings.

facts.title: The Palace of Mirrors
facts.description: Sheesh Mahal takes its name from the extensive use of tiny pieces of glass and mirror decoration across its interior surfaces.

facts.title: Part of the Imperial Bath Complex
facts.description: The chambers formed part of the royal palace and bathing complex created during Shah Jahan's reign.

facts.title: Light Once Made the Walls Sparkle
facts.description: The mirror mosaics were designed to catch artificial light, creating a glittering effect across the otherwise enclosed chambers.

items: Interior access may be restricted for conservation
View decorative work only from permitted areas
Do not touch fragile historic surfaces
groups.title: At Sheesh Mahal

audio.title: Sheesh Mahal: The Palace of Mirrors

description: Sheesh Mahal, or the Palace of Mirrors, is a Shah Jahan-era structure associated with the imperial bath complex. Its walls and ceilings were decorated with intricate glass mosaic work designed to shimmer dramatically in reflected light.

facts.title: A 119-Acre Garden
facts.description: Akbar's mausoleum stands within a vast 119-acre garden, making the landscape an essential part of the monument's design.

facts.title: Designed as a Charbagh
facts.description: The garden follows the traditional four-part charbagh plan, with causeways and water channels dividing the landscape into ordered sections.

facts.title: Blackbuck Still Roam Here
facts.description: The gardens of Sikandra are known for blackbuck that can still be seen moving through the grounds alongside peacocks and other wildlife.

items: Observe wildlife from a respectful distance
Look along the central axis toward the mausoleum
Do not feed blackbuck, monkeys or other animals
groups.title: At the Charbagh

description: The Charbagh surrounding Akbar's Tomb is a vast four-part Mughal garden organized around pathways, causeways and water channels. The mausoleum rises at its centre, turning the landscape into a carefully planned setting for the emperor's final resting place.

facts.title: Why It Is Called Kanch Mahal
facts.description: The building became known as Kanch Mahal because colourful glazed tiles were extensively used in its decoration, traces of which still survive.

facts.title: A Rare Mughal Residence
facts.description: Unlike the nearby mausoleum, Kanch Mahal is an example of Mughal domestic architecture, with rooms, balconies and a central hall designed as a residential palace.

facts.title: Its Exact Royal Role Is Debated
facts.description: Historical traditions associate Kanch Mahal with the royal household and with Jahangir's hunting visits, but its precise original use is not known with complete certainty.

items: Notice the carved floral and geometric sandstone panels
Do not touch fragile decorative surfaces
groups.title: At Kanch Mahal

description: Kanch Mahal stands near the southeast corner of Akbar's Tomb complex and is a rare surviving example of Mughal domestic architecture. The two-storeyed structure is richly carved in red sandstone and once carried colourful glazed-tile decoration. Historical traditions connect it with the royal household and Jahangir's hunting visits.

facts.title: Akbar Planned His Own Tomb
facts.description: Akbar selected the site and began work on his own mausoleum, but he died before its completion. His son Jahangir completed it in 1613.

facts.title: A Pyramid Instead of a Dome
facts.description: Unlike many famous Mughal tombs, Akbar's mausoleum rises through a series of receding levels rather than being crowned by one enormous central dome.

facts.title: The Real Grave Lies Below
facts.description: The white-marble cenotaph belongs to the symbolic upper arrangement, while Akbar's actual grave lies in the burial chamber reached through the lower part of the mausoleum.

items: Touching paintings, carvings or historic surfaces
groups.title: What Not to Do

items: Maintain a respectful atmosphere near the burial chamber
Look at the decorated vestibule before entering the grave chamber
Upper levels are generally not part of the normal visitor route
Follow ASI barriers and visitor instructions
groups.title: Inside the Mausoleum

audio.title: Akbar's Tomb: An Emperor's Final Vision

description: Akbar's Main Mausoleum stands at the centre of the Sikandra garden and rises as a series of receding red-sandstone levels crowned by an open white-marble pavilion. Akbar began the project himself, while his son Jahangir completed it after his death. The emperor's actual grave lies within the lower burial chamber.

facts.title: The Main Gateway
facts.description: Although Akbar's tomb complex has four monumental gateways, the southern gateway is the principal entrance and the grandest of the four.

facts.title: Four Marble Minarets
facts.description: Four slender white-marble minarets rise above the gateway, creating one of the complex's most distinctive architectural features.

facts.title: Red Sandstone Meets White Marble
facts.description: The gateway combines deep red sandstone with bold white-marble inlay, geometric patterns, floral decoration and calligraphy.

items: Pause before entering to notice the marble inlay and calligraphy
Look up at the four white-marble minarets
Expect security screening at the entrance
groups.title: At the Great South Gateway

audio.title: The Great Gateway to Akbar's Tomb

description: The Great South Gateway is the principal entrance to Akbar's tomb complex at Sikandra. Built in red sandstone and richly decorated with white-marble inlay, geometric designs and calligraphy, it is crowned by four distinctive marble minarets and prepares visitors for the monumental garden and mausoleum beyond.

facts.title: The Tomb Sits at the Centre
facts.description: Unlike the later Taj Mahal, I'timad-ud-Daulah's mausoleum follows the classic Mughal garden-tomb arrangement by standing near the centre of its charbagh.

facts.title: Four Equal Garden Quarters
facts.description: Raised pathways and water channels divide the garden into four main sections, following the traditional charbagh plan.

facts.title: Water Was Part of the Architecture
facts.description: The original garden design included water channels, pools, fountains and cascades rather than treating the landscape as simple greenery.

items: Damaging plants or historic water features
groups.title: What Not to Do

items: Look along the main axis to understand the garden's symmetry
Notice the surviving water channels and geometric layout
groups.title: At the Charbagh

audio.title: Charbagh: The Garden Around the Jewel Box

description: The Charbagh forms the landscaped setting of I'timad-ud-Daulah's Tomb. Raised pathways and water channels divide the garden into four principal quarters, while the white-marble mausoleum occupies the centre of the carefully ordered composition.

facts.title: The Main Entrance
facts.description: The eastern gateway serves as the principal entrance to the tomb complex, leading visitors directly toward the central mausoleum.

facts.title: Marble Patterns on Red Sandstone
facts.description: The gateway combines red sandstone with bold white-marble inlay, previewing the decorative techniques used extensively on the mausoleum.

facts.title: Part of a Symmetrical Plan
facts.description: Gateway-like structures were placed on the other sides of the garden to maintain the symmetry of the four-part Mughal garden.

items: Pause to notice the white-marble inlay on red sandstone
Look through the gateway toward the main mausoleum
Do not touch or damage decorative surfaces
groups.title: At the East Gateway

audio.title: East Gateway: Entering the Baby Taj

description: The East Gateway is the principal entrance to I'timad-ud-Daulah's tomb complex. Built in red sandstone and decorated with white-marble inlay, it introduces visitors to the geometric and floral decoration that becomes even more elaborate on the mausoleum ahead.

facts.title: A Daughter Built It for Her Father
facts.description: Empress Nur Jahan commissioned the mausoleum for her father Mirza Ghiyas Beg, who had received the title I'timad-ud-Daulah, meaning 'Pillar of the State'.

facts.title: A Turning Point in Mughal Architecture
facts.description: The monument is regarded as the first Mughal structure built entirely in white marble and among the earliest to use colourful stone inlay so extensively.

facts.title: A Jewel Box of Stone
facts.description: Semi-precious stones form images of flowers, cypress trees, fruit, vessels and other delicate motifs across the marble surfaces.

items: Touching marble inlay or jali screens
groups.title: What Not to Do

items: Respect the monument as a burial place
Look carefully at the marble jali screens and stone inlay
Do not touch fragile decorative surfaces
groups.title: Inside the Mausoleum

description: The Main Mausoleum of I'timad-ud-Daulah was commissioned by Empress Nur Jahan for her father Mirza Ghiyas Beg and also commemorates her mother Asmat Begum. Completed in 1628, the white-marble tomb marks an important transition in Mughal architecture through its extensive coloured-stone inlay, delicate jali screens and richly painted interiors.

facts.title: The Garden Once Opened to the River
facts.description: The western pavilion faces the Yamuna and formed an important riverfront element of the tomb complex.

facts.title: More Than a Decorative Gateway
facts.description: Unlike the simpler ornamental structures on the north and south sides, the western building contains substantial rooms and is interpreted as a pleasure pavilion.

facts.title: Agra's Monuments Faced the Yamuna
facts.description: The pavilion reflects the Mughal tradition of building gardens and palaces along the river, where the Yamuna formed an important part of the architectural setting.

items: Look toward the Yamuna to understand the original riverfront setting
Do not cross barriers near the river-facing edge
groups.title: At the Riverfront Pavilion

audio.title: Riverfront Pavilion: The Tomb and the Yamuna

description: The Riverfront Pavilion stands on the western side of I'timad-ud-Daulah's garden overlooking the Yamuna. Larger and more substantial than the ornamental side gateways, it reflects the Mughal riverfront tradition in which gardens, palaces and tombs were closely connected with the river.

facts.title: The Taj Changes Color
facts.description: It appears pink in the morning, bright white in the day, and golden at sunset due to sunlight reflecting on the marble.

facts.title: Almost Perfectly Symmetrical
facts.description: The entire complex is symmetrical except one detail: Shah Jahan’s tomb is slightly off-center next to Mumtaz Mahal’s.

facts.title: Optical Illusion in Calligraphy
facts.description: The Quranic calligraphy looks uniform, but the letters are bigger at the top so it appears perfectly aligned from the ground.

items: Shoe covers are mandatory or footwear must be removed
No touching or scratching marble surfaces
groups.title: Inside Mausoleum Rules

description: Contrary to popular belief, the Great Wall of China cannot be seen from the Moon with the naked eye. It can be seen from low Earth orbit under perfect conditions.

facts.title: Its Name Means Peerless Pool
facts.description: Anup Talao is commonly interpreted as the 'Peerless Pool', reflecting its special place within Akbar's private palace courtyard.

facts.title: An Island at the Centre
facts.description: A square stone platform stands in the middle of the water tank and is connected to the surrounding courtyard by four narrow bridges.

facts.title: At the Heart of the Private Palace
facts.description: The pool is surrounded by some of Fatehpur Sikri's most important private buildings, including Akbar's Khwabgah and other royal pavilions.

items: Notice the four bridges meeting at the central platform
Look around at the surrounding palace buildings
Do not enter restricted portions of the pool
groups.title: At Anup Talao

description: Anup Talao is a square ornamental water tank within Akbar's private palace complex. Its most distinctive feature is a central stone platform connected to the surrounding courtyard by four narrow bridges, placing the pool at the visual centre of several royal buildings.

facts.title: The Name Comes with a Question Mark
facts.description: The building is traditionally called Birbal's House, but historians do not treat its association with Akbar's famous courtier Birbal as completely certain.

facts.title: Small but Exceptionally Ornate
facts.description: Despite its modest size, the building is among Fatehpur Sikri's most richly carved residential structures.

facts.title: Stone Made to Look Like Wood
facts.description: Its elaborate brackets, beams and carved details demonstrate how Mughal craftsmen translated forms associated with timber architecture into red sandstone.

items: Look closely at the carved brackets and stone beams
Remember that the traditional building name does not prove Birbal lived here
groups.title: At Birbal's House

audio.title: Birbal's House: A Palace with a Question

description: Birbal's House is the traditional name given to one of Fatehpur Sikri's most ornate small residential buildings. Its richly carved red-sandstone brackets, beams and decorative details make it architecturally important, although the identification of the building specifically as Birbal's residence is not certain.

facts.title: A Gate Built for Victory
facts.description: Buland Darwaza was completed in 1575 to commemorate Emperor Akbar's victory in Gujarat.

facts.title: Gateway to the Great Mosque
facts.description: Rather than serving as the entrance to a palace, Buland Darwaza forms the monumental southern entrance to the Jama Masjid courtyard.

facts.title: Designed to Overwhelm
facts.description: Its enormous scale, high flight of steps and towering central arch make the gateway appear even more imposing when approached from below.

items: Be prepared for a long flight of steps
Pause below the gateway to appreciate its scale
Follow ASI and mosque visitor instructions
groups.title: At Buland Darwaza

audio.title: Buland Darwaza: Akbar's Gate of Victory

description: Buland Darwaza is the monumental southern gateway of the Jama Masjid at Fatehpur Sikri. Emperor Akbar commissioned it to commemorate his Gujarat campaign, turning a functional entrance into one of the most dramatic architectural statements of his reign.

facts.title: Akbar's Public Court
facts.description: Diwan-i-Am was the Hall of Public Audience where the emperor heard petitions and conducted affairs before assembled subjects.

facts.title: Not Only a Courtroom
facts.description: The large courtyard was also used for celebrations and, during part of Akbar's reign, public prayers.

facts.title: The Emperor Sat Apart
facts.description: A raised pavilion on the western side provided the emperor with a distinct throne space overlooking the courtyard.

items: Look across the courtyard toward the emperor's throne pavilion
Do not climb on historic platforms
groups.title: At Diwan-i-Am

description: Diwan-i-Am was Akbar's Hall of Public Audience at Fatehpur Sikri. A broad rectangular courtyard surrounded by cloisters allowed subjects, officials and visitors to assemble while the emperor occupied a raised throne pavilion.

facts.title: One Extraordinary Central Pillar
facts.description: The interior is dominated by a richly carved central stone column whose enormous bracketed capital supports a circular platform.

facts.title: Four Bridges Lead to the Centre
facts.description: Four narrow stone passages connect the central platform with the corners of the chamber, producing one of Fatehpur Sikri's most unusual interiors.

facts.title: Also Known as the Jewel House
facts.description: UNESCO notes that the building is also known as the Jewel House, reflecting uncertainty about the exact function of this extraordinary structure.

items: Look upward at the central column and its bracketed capital
Notice the four stone passages radiating from the centre
Do not climb on historic structures
groups.title: At Diwan-i-Khas

audio.title: Diwan-i-Khas: The Mystery of the Central Pillar

description: Diwan-i-Khas is one of Fatehpur Sikri's most distinctive buildings. Its apparently two-storeyed exterior surrounds a single chamber dominated by an elaborately carved central column, a circular platform and four narrow stone passages extending toward the corners.

facts.title: The City Grew Around the Mosque
facts.description: Jama Masjid was among the earliest major buildings at Fatehpur Sikri, completed in 1571-1572 as Akbar's new capital was taking shape.

facts.title: One of India's Great Mosques
facts.description: The enormous congregational courtyard and prayer hall made Jama Masjid one of the most important Mughal mosques of its period.

facts.title: A Living Religious Complex
facts.description: Unlike many palace buildings at Fatehpur Sikri, Jama Masjid continues to function as a place of worship and pilgrimage.

audio.title: Jama Masjid: The Spiritual Beginning of Fatehpur Sikri

description: Jama Masjid is the great congregational mosque of Fatehpur Sikri and one of the earliest major monuments constructed in Akbar's new capital. Its enormous courtyard later became the setting for the marble Tomb of Sheikh Salim Chishti and the monumental Buland Darwaza.

facts.title: The Largest Royal Residence
facts.description: The Palace of Jodha Bai is the largest building within Fatehpur Sikri's residential palace complex.

facts.title: Privacy Was Built into the Architecture
facts.description: High surrounding walls and a guarded eastern gateway separated the residential courtyard from the more public areas of the imperial city.

facts.title: Several Traditions Meet Here
facts.description: Its carved pillars, balconies, screens, cupolas and other details combine architectural traditions from different regions of India with Mughal forms.

items: Climbing onto balconies or restricted structures
groups.title: What Not to Do

items: Enter the central courtyard to understand the residential plan
Look closely at carved pillars and stone screens
Remain within permitted rooms and passages
groups.title: At the Palace

audio.title: Jodha Bai's Palace: Life Inside Akbar's Royal Court

description: The Palace of Jodha Bai is the largest residential building in Fatehpur Sikri's imperial palace complex. Built around a spacious enclosed courtyard, its architecture combines richly carved pillars, balconies, stone screens and domed elements drawn from several architectural traditions.

facts.title: Akbar's Bedchamber
facts.description: Khwabgah means 'House of Dreams' and refers to the private upper-level bedchamber within Akbar's residential quarters.

facts.title: His Library Was Below
facts.description: The ground-floor rooms included Akbar's library and a larger private resting area, placing intellectual and private life within the same palace complex.

facts.title: Connected to the Royal Residence
facts.description: Corridors connected the Khwabgah complex with several nearby residential buildings, including Panch Mahal and the palace traditionally called Jodha Bai's.

items: Look for surviving traces of painted decoration
Notice its close relationship with Anup Talao
Some chambers may have restricted access
groups.title: At Khwabgah

description: Khwabgah formed part of Emperor Akbar's private residential apartments beside Anup Talao. The lower rooms included his library and resting space, while the upper level contained the imperial bedchamber and was linked by corridors with other parts of the royal residential complex.

facts.title: Five Levels, Each Smaller Than the Last
facts.description: Panch Mahal rises through five progressively smaller open levels, giving the building its distinctive pyramidal appearance.

facts.title: Built Almost Entirely from Columns
facts.description: Instead of enclosed rooms, the pavilion relies on rows of carved stone columns, making it unusually open and airy.

facts.title: Architecture Designed for Air
facts.description: UNESCO compares its open tiered design to a Persian badgir or wind-catching structure, well suited to shade and ventilation.

items: Stand back to appreciate all five levels together
Notice how each floor becomes progressively smaller
groups.title: At Panch Mahal

audio.title: Panch Mahal: Akbar's Palace of Five Levels

description: Panch Mahal is a remarkable five-storey red-sandstone pavilion composed largely of open colonnades. Each successive level becomes smaller until the building ends in a single chhatri, producing an airy structure unlike the enclosed palaces surrounding it.

facts.title: The Saint Behind Akbar's City
facts.description: Akbar deeply revered Sheikh Salim Chishti, the Sufi saint whose blessing was associated with the birth of Akbar's heir, Prince Salim.

facts.title: White Marble Among Red Sandstone
facts.description: The tomb's luminous white-marble appearance creates a striking contrast with the red sandstone of the surrounding Jama Masjid.

facts.title: A Living Place of Pilgrimage
facts.description: The shrine remains an active devotional destination where visitors continue longstanding traditions of prayer and remembrance.

items: Photography rules may vary inside the shrine
groups.title: At the Shrine

audio.title: Sheikh Salim Chishti: The Saint Behind Sikri

description: The Tomb of Sheikh Salim Chishti is a white-marble Sufi shrine standing within the courtyard of Jama Masjid. Akbar built the mausoleum in honour of the saint whose prophecy and blessing became closely connected with the birth of his heir, Prince Salim, the future Emperor Jahangir.

audio.title: Ram Bagh Gateways: Entering Babur's Garden

description: The historic gateways of Ram Bagh formed part of the larger Mughal garden complex on the Yamuna. They survive alongside the garden's pavilions, terraces and other protected architectural remains and mark the transition into one of Agra's earliest Mughal landscapes.

facts.title: Part of the Protected Ram Bagh Complex
facts.description: ASI's official monument records include the Katra together with Ram Bagh's houses, kiosks and terraces.

facts.title: Ram Bagh Was More Than a Garden
facts.description: The presence of residential and service structures shows that Ram Bagh functioned as a larger architectural complex rather than simply as landscaped lawns.

facts.title: Its Historic Fabric Still Matters
facts.description: Archaeological conservation records document repair work specifically on the Gateway and Katra at Ram Bagh.

items: Some historic sections may have restricted access
Observe surviving rooms and gateways from permitted areas
Do not climb on damaged masonry
groups.title: At the Katra

audio.title: The Katra: Ram Bagh Beyond the Garden

description: The Katra forms part of the protected architectural remains associated with Ram Bagh. Together with surviving houses, kiosks, gateways and terraces, it shows that the historic site contained functional built spaces in addition to its celebrated gardens and waterworks.

facts.title: Designed to Face the Yamuna
facts.description: Two viewing pavilions were positioned toward the river, making the Yamuna an important part of the garden experience.

facts.title: A Natural Mughal Air Conditioner
facts.description: The pavilion complex incorporates subterranean tahkhana chambers that provided a cooler retreat during Agra's intense summer heat.

facts.title: Water and Architecture Worked Together
facts.description: The pavilions were integrated with Ram Bagh's terraces, water channels, tanks and cascades to create a cooler riverfront environment.

items: Look toward the Yamuna to understand the original setting
Notice how the pavilions connect with the water system
groups.title: At the Riverfront Pavilions

audio.title: Riverfront Pavilions: How the Mughals Beat Agra's Heat

description: Ram Bagh's surviving riverfront pavilions overlook the Yamuna and formed part of the garden's carefully engineered cooling landscape. Their associated subterranean tahkhana chambers provided relief during the hot summer months, while nearby water channels and terraces helped create a cooler environment.

facts.title: The Garden Works on Three Levels
facts.description: Ram Bagh's landscape was arranged across three principal levels, combining planted areas with terraces, tanks and architectural structures.

facts.title: Water Was the Garden's Cooling System
facts.description: Water drawn from the Yamuna moved through channels, tanks, fountains and cascades, helping cool the garden as well as beautify it.

facts.title: Stone Chutes Changed the Sound of Water
facts.description: Historical descriptions record specially shaped stone water chutes that broke the flowing water and created a gentle gurgling sound.

year_built: From c. 1528, with later Mughal modifications

items: Follow the water channels through the different garden levels
Notice surviving tanks, channels and stone water chutes
Some fountains may not be operational
groups.title: At the Water Terraces

description: Ram Bagh was designed around an elaborate relationship between landscape and water. Its terraced levels incorporated channels, fountains, tanks and cascades that distributed Yamuna water through the garden while helping create a cooler environment during Agra's hot summers.

facts.title: A Garden Inspired by Paradise
facts.description: The Charbagh follows the Persian-Timurid tradition of dividing a garden into four parts, symbolically associated with the gardens and rivers of Paradise.

facts.title: The Taj Breaks a Mughal Tradition
facts.description: Earlier Mughal garden tombs commonly placed the mausoleum near the centre of the garden. At the Taj Mahal, the tomb stands dramatically at the northern riverfront edge.

facts.title: Water Was Central to the Design
facts.description: Water from the Yamuna was historically carried into the garden and distributed through channels and underground pipes to supply its pools and fountains.

items: Pause near the central water axis to understand the garden's symmetry
Avoid damaging lawns, plants or heritage surfaces

facts.description: Chini Ka Rauza is especially remarkable for its Persian-style glazed tile decoration, known as kashi or chini work, once covering much of the monument.

facts.description: Two main walkways divide the Charbagh into four large quadrants, and smaller cross-paths divide them again to create sixteen garden sections.
facts.title: Four Gardens Become Sixteen

facts.description: The Charbagh follows a Persian-Mughal paradise-garden tradition in which four divisions and flowing water symbolically evoke the rivers and gardens of paradise.
facts.title: The Garden Represents Paradise
The Famous Benches Came Later
facts.description: The marble platform at the garden's center originally featured an ornamental pool with five fountains. The four marble benches around it were added in 1907-08 during Lord Curzon's period.

items: Do not damage plants or historic structures
Keep the garden and water channels clean
groups.title: While Exploring the Garden

description: The Taj Mahal Charbagh is the formal Mughal garden stretching between the Great Gate and the mausoleum. Its cross-axial pathways divide the garden into four principal sections and sixteen smaller plots, while the central water channels, fountains and reflecting pool reinforce the symmetry of the entire Taj Mahal composition. Its design draws on the Persian-Mughal concept of the garden of paradise.

facts.description: The Mughal chronicler Lahauri called it Darwaza-i-Rauza, meaning the 'Gate of the Mausoleum'. It marks the transition from the Jilaukhana forecourt into the funerary garden.
facts.title: Its Name Means 'Gate of the Mausoleum'
Its Calligraphy Welcomes You Toward Paradise
facts.description: Quranic calligraphy in black marble decorates the Great Gate. The inscription evokes peace, return to God and entry into Paradise, setting the spiritual tone before visitors enter the garden.

facts.title: Its Architecture Prepares You for the Taj
facts.description: The gateway uses a monumental central pishtaq flanked by two tiers of niches, creating a grand architectural introduction before the white-marble mausoleum is revealed beyond it.

items: Avoid touching or scratching the historic surfaces

Keep your phone on silent inside the Taj complex
groups.title: At the Great Gate

description: Darwaza-i-Rauza is the monumental Great Gate that separates the Taj Mahal's ceremonial forecourt from its funerary garden. Built in red sandstone with white-marble detailing and Quranic calligraphy, the gateway was designed to create a dramatic transition before visitors encounter the mausoleum beyond.

facts.title: The Gate of the Mausoleum
facts.description: The historic name Darwaza-i Rauza means 'Gate of the Mausoleum'. It marks the transition from Jilaukhana into the formal funerary garden of the Taj Mahal.

facts.title: Amanat Khan Left His Signature
facts.description: The gateway's calligraphy is associated with master calligrapher Amanat Khan. An inscription on the gateway includes his signature and a date corresponding to 1647-1648.

facts.title: Designed to Prepare You for the Taj
facts.description: The Great Gate was designed as a monumental transition. Passing through its central arch gradually frames and reveals the white-marble mausoleum beyond.

groups.title: At the Great Gate

audio.title: Great Gate: The Gateway to the Taj

description: The Great Gate, historically known as Darwaza-i Rauza, stands between Jilaukhana and the Taj Mahal's Charbagh garden. Built primarily of red sandstone with white-marble detailing, the monumental gateway prepares visitors for the mausoleum ahead. Its large central arch, geometric decoration and Quranic calligraphy make it an important architectural work in its own right.

facts.title: A Ceremonial Waiting Ground
facts.description: Visitors once dismounted from their horses and elephants here and assembled before proceeding through the Great Gate into the Taj Mahal's funerary garden.

facts.title: Its Name Describes Its Location
facts.description: The name Jilaukhana literally means 'in front of the house', reflecting its role as the forecourt before the main Taj Mahal complex.

facts.title: More Than Just an Entrance
facts.description: The forecourt is surrounded by historic structures, including the Khawasspuras, once used by tomb attendants, and the Saheli Burj tomb complexes.

groups.title: At Jilaukhana

description: Jilaukhana is the ceremonial forecourt of the Taj Mahal, positioned between the outer entrance gates and the Great Gate. In the Mughal period, visitors dismounted from horses and elephants here and assembled according to imperial court etiquette before entering the funerary garden.

facts.description: Jilaukhana literally means 'in front of the house'. It served as the formal forecourt visitors passed through before entering the Taj Mahal's main garden.
facts.title: Its Name Means 'In Front of the House'
Visitors Once Arrived Here on Horses and Elephants
facts.description: During the Mughal period, visitors would dismount from horses and elephants here and assemble before proceeding through the Great Gate.
Jilaukhana was not simply an entrance space. Its architecture created an ordered setting for court etiquette, processions and the ceremonial approach to the mausoleum.
facts.title: It Was Designed for Mughal Ceremony

description: Jilaukhana is the large ceremonial forecourt immediately before the Great Gate of the Taj Mahal. During the Mughal period, visitors gathered here after dismounting from horses and elephants before entering the funerary garden. Surrounded by subsidiary courtyards and connected to the historic bazaar streets, it formed an important stage in the carefully planned approach to the Taj Mahal.

facts.title: The Graves Are Actually Below
facts.description: The decorated monuments visitors see in the central chamber are cenotaphs. The actual graves of Mumtaz Mahal and Shah Jahan lie in a lower tomb chamber.

facts.title: One Detail Breaks the Symmetry
facts.description: Mumtaz Mahal's cenotaph occupies the centre of the chamber. Shah Jahan's larger cenotaph was later placed beside hers, creating the most famous break in the Taj Mahal's symmetry.

facts.title: Flowers Made from Stone
facts.description: The interior is decorated with intricate floral designs made using coloured and semi-precious stones carefully inlaid into white marble.

items: Shoe covers or be prepared to remove footwear

audio.title: Inside the Heart of the Taj Mahal

description: The Main Mausoleum is the architectural and emotional centre of the Taj Mahal complex. Clad entirely in white marble, it houses the richly decorated cenotaphs of Mumtaz Mahal and Shah Jahan in its central chamber, while their actual graves lie in a lower chamber beneath.

facts.title: 569 Prayer Spaces Are Marked on the Floor
facts.description: The mosque floor contains the outlines of 569 prayer rugs picked out in black marble, creating clearly defined spaces for worshippers.
Although Mihman Khana mirrors it on the eastern side, the western building is a functioning mosque with architectural features specifically designed for prayer and sermons.
facts.title: The Mosque Gives the Complex Its Religious Function

facts.description: The mosque came first in the architectural logic of the riverfront ensemble. Mihman Khana on the opposite side was designed as its visual counterpart, or 'jawab', to preserve the Taj Mahal's symmetry.
facts.title: Mihman Khana Was Built to Mirror It

items: Respect the mosque as an active place of worship

groups.title: Inside Mausoleum Rules

description: The Masjid stands on the western side of the Taj Mahal's main mausoleum and forms an essential part of the riverfront ensemble. Built primarily in red sandstone, it gives the complex an active religious function while balancing the Mihman Khana on the eastern side. Its prayer hall is divided into three sections beneath domed vaults, and the floor is marked with hundreds of individual prayer spaces in black marble.

facts.title: The Mosque's Architectural Answer
facts.description: Mihman Khana mirrors the mosque on the opposite side of the mausoleum, creating the bilateral symmetry that defines the Taj Mahal complex.

facts.title: A Hall for Memorial Gatherings
facts.description: The building accommodated visitors attending observances marking the death anniversary of Mumtaz Mahal after earlier gatherings had been held in tents.

facts.title: Architects Left Drawings in Stone
facts.description: Two working drawings showing the silhouette of the mausoleum's finial were scratched into stone slabs on the Mihman Khana platform.

Look for the architectural working drawings on the platform

description: Four tall marble minarets stand at the corners of the mausoleum platform and frame the Taj Mahal from every direction. Their repeated balconies, slender proportions and crowning chhatris strengthen the symmetry of the entire composition.

groups.title: At the Riverfront Terrace

audio.title: The Taj Mahal and the Yamuna

description: The Riverfront Terrace is the enormous platform along the Yamuna that supports the Taj Mahal's central riverfront composition. The mausoleum occupies its centre, with the mosque to the west and Mihman Khana to the east. Its scale allowed Shah Jahan's architects to transform the Mughal riverfront-garden tradition into a monumental funerary complex.
